{{Short description|Mathematical puzzle}}
[[File:String_girdling_Earth.svg|thumb|300px|Visualisation showing that the length added to the circumference (blue) is dependent only on the additional radius (red) and not the original circumference (grey)]]
'''String girdling Earth''' is a mathematical puzzle with a [[counterintuitive]] solution. In a version of this puzzle, string is tightly wrapped around the equator of a perfectly spherical Earth. If the string should be raised 1 metre (roughly 3 ft 3 in) off the ground, all the way along the equator, how much longer would the string be?

Alternatively, {{convert|1|m}} of string is spliced into the original string, and the extended string rearranged so that it is at a uniform height above the equator. The question that is then posed is whether the gap between string and Earth will allow the passage of a car, a cat or a thin knife blade.

==Solution==
[[File:String_girdling_square.svg|thumb|Visual analogue using a square showing that additional string is added only at the corners: four circular arcs adding up to a circle with radius equal to the offset]]
As the string must be raised all along the entire {{convert|40000|km|abbr=on|adj=on}} circumference, one might expect several kilometres of additional string. Surprisingly, the answer is 2{{pi}} m or around {{convert|6.3|m}}.

In the second phrasing, considering that {{convert|1|m}} is almost negligible compared with the {{convert|40000|km|abbr=on|adj=on}} circumference, the first response may be that the new position of the string will be no different from the original surface-hugging position. The answer is that a cat will easily pass through the gap, the size of which will be {{sfrac|1|2{{pi}} }} metres or about {{convert|16|cm|abbr=on}}.

Even more surprising is that the size of the sphere or circle around which the string is spanned is irrelevant, and may be anything from the size of an atom to the [[Milky Way]] &mdash; the result depends only on the amount it is raised. Moreover, as in the [[coin_rotation_paradox#Unequal_radii_and_other_shapes|coin-rolling problem]], the shape the string girdles need not be a circle: 2{{pi}} times the offset is added when it is any [[simple polygon]] or closed curve which does not intersect itself. If the shape is [[complex polygon|complex]], 2{{pi}} times the offset, times the absolute value of its [[winding number|turning number]] must be added.<ref>{{cite book
|title=The world of mathematics, Volume 4
|first1=James Roy
|last1=Newman
|publisher=Courier Dover Publications
|year=2000
|isbn=0-486-41152-4
|page=2436
|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YgmDjp9OAPMC}}, [https://books.google.com/books?id=YgmDjp9OAPMC&pg=PA2436 p. 2436]
</ref>

This diagram gives a visual analogue using a square: regardless of the size of the square, the added perimeter is the sum of the four blue arcs, a circle with the same radius as the offset.

More formally, let ''c''&thinsp; be the Earth's circumference, ''r''&thinsp; its radius, ''&Delta;c''&thinsp; the added string length and ''&Delta;r''&thinsp; the added radius. {{nowrap|As a circle of radius ''R''&thinsp;}} has a circumference of 2{{pi}}''R''&thinsp;,

{{ Annotated image
 | image   = 400m_com_barreira_masculino_(21372346524).jpg
 | caption = Photograph showing the offset between starting lines of an athletics track
 | width   = 200 | height = 200 | image-width = 360 | image-left = -55 | image-top = -33
}}

:<math>
\begin{align}
      c       + \varDelta c & = 2 \pi (r +       \varDelta r)
\\    2 \pi r + \varDelta c & = 2 \pi  r + 2 \pi \varDelta r
\\              \varDelta c & =            2 \pi \varDelta r
\\ \therefore\; \varDelta r & = \frac{\varDelta c}{2 \pi}
\end{align}
</math>

regardless of the value of ''c''&thinsp;.

==Implications==

This observation means that an athletics track has the same offset between starting lines on each lane, equal to 2{{pi}} times the width of the lane, whether the circumference of the inside lane is the standard {{convert|400|m|abbr=on}} or the size of a galaxy.

As aircraft fly at high altitude [[fuel_economy_in_aircraft#Altitude|to save fuel due to lower drag]], the formula shows that a ''&Delta;a'' rise in altitude lengthens a flight along an entire [[great circle]] by 2{{pi}}&thinsp;''&Delta;a''. For example, each additional [[flight level|1000 feet]] adds 2 &times; {{pi}} &times; 1000 &asymp; 6283 feet (about 1 [[nautical mile]]) around the whole Earth. In [[International System of Units|SI units]], each kilometre altitude increases the distance by 15.7 cm, per kilometre travelled. The higher efficiency far exceeds the negligible distance added.<ref>Australian Research &amp; Space Exploration, [http://spaceaustralia.com.au/blogs/news/why-do-planes-fly-at-high-altitude-meaning-its-a-further-distance ''Why do planes fly at high altitude meaning its a further distance? ''], May 7, 2024</ref>
